summary: Earlier LDAP specs did not say precisely how to compare character strings, causing usability and interoperability problems. This document defines string preparation algorithms for character-based matching rules. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: Before comparing two names, tidy them the same way, so Cafe and cafe written differently still match.

questions: how does ldap case ignore matching work
how does ldap handle spaces in matching
subtitle: The six-step recipe LDAP uses to clean up text so that strings written differently can still match.

tldr.problem: Earlier LDAP specifications did not say precisely how to compare character strings, which caused usability and interoperability problems.
tldr.mechanism: Every presented and stored value goes through a six-step process (transcode, map, normalize, prohibit, check bidi, insignificant character handling), based on stringprep, before matching.
tldr.outcome: Matching rules such as caseIgnoreMatch now behave the same everywhere, and a failure in any step makes the assertion evaluate to Undefined.

today: RFC 4518 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It is an integral part of the LDAP technical specification in RFC 4510.

sections.title: Why LDAP Needed Precise String Matching
sections.content:
An LDAP matching rule decides whether a presented value matches an attribute value. The answer can be True, False or Undefined (it cannot be determined). For example, caseIgnoreMatch can check whether the commonName attribute holds a value, ignoring case and insignificant spaces.

The X.520 definition of such rules is inadequate for Unicode strings. An implementation that folds lowercase to uppercase can give different results from one that folds uppercase to lowercase, and one implementation may treat only SPACE (U+0020) as a space while another treats every character with the space separator (Zs) property as one. The RFC notes that this caused interoperability problems and, in certificate chain validation, security vulnerabilities.
sections.eli5: If two people disagree on what counts as a space or a capital letter, they will disagree on whether two names match. This RFC gets everyone to follow the same rules.

sections.title: Relationship to Stringprep
sections.content:
The algorithms refine the stringprep approach of RFC 3454, where presented and stored values are first prepared so that a character-by-character comparison gives the correct result. Two extra steps are added: before the Unicode preparation, the string is transcoded to Unicode, and after it, the string is adjusted to handle characters that are insignificant to the matching rule.

The document is part of the LDAP technical specification (RFC 4510), which obsoletes RFC 3377 in its entirety. It is used by RFC 4517 and possibly other specifications that define LDAP syntaxes or matching rules. The tables in the RFC are definitive for implementing it, even though they derive from Unicode data.
sections.eli5: It borrows an existing tidying recipe and adds a step at the start and one at the end to fit what directories need.

sections.title: The Six-Step Process
sections.content:
The process SHALL be applied to each presented and attribute value before a character string matching rule is evaluated. Failure in any step causes the assertion to evaluate to Undefined. The character repertoire is Unicode 3.2. Implementations may use another process as long as the matching behavior is consistent with the one described.

The steps are Transcode, Map, Normalize, Prohibit, Check bidi and Insignificant Character Handling, as shown in the table below.
sections.eli5: Every name goes down the same assembly line of six stations, and if it gets stuck at any station, the answer is simply 'cannot tell'.

sections.title: Transcode, Map, Normalize, Prohibit and Bidi
sections.content:
Transcode: non-Unicode strings are converted to Unicode. PrintableString is transcoded directly, UniversalString, UTF8String and bmpString need no transcoding, and TeletexString is converted by a local mapping because no standard exists. Use of TeletexString is NOT RECOMMENDED.

Map: SOFT HYPHEN (U+00AD), MONGOLIAN TODO SOFT HYPHEN (U+1806), COMBINING GRAPHEME JOINER (U+034F), the variation selectors and OBJECT REPLACEMENT CHARACTER (U+FFFC) are mapped to nothing. Tab, line feed, line tabulation, form feed, carriage return and NEXT LINE (NEL) become SPACE (U+0020). Other control and format code points are mapped to nothing, ZERO WIDTH SPACE (U+200B) is mapped to nothing, and other separator code points (Zs, Zl, Zp) become SPACE. For case ignore, numeric and stored prefix string rules, characters are also case folded per B.2 of RFC 3454.

Normalize: the string is converted to Unicode Form KC (compatibility composed).

Prohibit: the step fails if the string contains unassigned code points, characters that change display properties or are deprecated, private use code points, non-character code points, surrogate codes or the REPLACEMENT CHARACTER (U+FFFD).

Check bidi: bidirectional characters are ignored.
sections.eli5: First everything is put into one alphabet, invisible junk is thrown away, odd spaces become ordinary spaces, and capitals are made small. Then strange or forbidden symbols make the whole check fail.

sections.title: Insignificant Character Handling
sections.content:
The last step depends on the matching rule. For case ignore and exact string matching, a space is a SPACE (U+0020) not followed by combining marks. For attribute values and non-substring assertion values, a string with no non-space character becomes exactly two SPACEs. Otherwise it starts and ends with exactly one SPACE, and every inner run of spaces becomes exactly two SPACEs. So foo<SPACE>bar<SPACE><SPACE> becomes <SPACE>foo<SPACE><SPACE>bar<SPACE>.

For substring assertion values, a string of only spaces becomes exactly one SPACE, and the start and end are padded depending on whether the piece is an initial, any or final substring.

For numericString matching, all spaces are removed. For telephoneNumber matching, all hyphens (several hyphen and minus code points are listed) and spaces are removed, so a string of only hyphens becomes empty.
sections.eli5: Extra spaces are tidied: people often type too many, so the extras are squeezed. In phone and number fields, spaces and dashes are simply thrown away.

sections.title: Why Substring Matching Shapes the Space Rules
sections.content:
Appendix B explains why the space handling is not simpler. If all runs of spaces were collapsed to one and leading and trailing spaces dropped, substring filters would misbehave. For instance, (CN=foo\20*\20bar) would match the value foobar, and (CN=*\20foobar\20*) would match foobar while (CN=*\20*foobar*\20*) would not.

X.520 says only leading, trailing and multiple consecutive spaces of the whole string are insignificant, not those of each substring. The RFC admits one anomaly: the assertion (CN=\20*\20*\20) matches neither a value of three spaces nor a single space. It judges this acceptable because simple assertions such as (cn=\20) cover the practical need.
sections.eli5: When you search for a name with a gap in the middle, the spaces around the gap really matter, so the rules had to be careful not to squash them.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The security considerations of RFC 3454 (stringprep) generally apply to these algorithms. The document adds no further security text of its own, beyond noting in its background that imprecise matching has led to vulnerabilities in certificate chain validation.
sections.eli5: It points to the safety advice of the recipe it borrowed from, because ambiguous matching can let the wrong thing slip through.

items.label: Map
items.desc: Drop or replace some characters and case fold where needed.

items.label: Insignificant Character Handling
items.desc: Adjust spaces, hyphens and similar per matching rule.
